stem:
Which of the following statements about the tropopause is/are correct?
Its height is maximum over the equator.
It acts as a barrier to vertical movement of air.
Its height remains constant throughout the year.
Select the correct answer using the code below:
solution:
Statement 1: the tropopause lies highest over the equator (about 18 km) and lowest over the poles (about 8 km), because the equatorial troposphere is deep and warm. Correct.
Statement 2: at the tropopause the fall of temperature ceases, so the layer is an isothermal cap that checks rising air and blocks vertical movement. Correct.
Statement 3: the height of the tropopause shifts with season and with surface temperature, so it is not constant through the year. Incorrect.
Correct statements: 1 and 2 only.
Matches option A.
subject: Geography

stem: The main reason for decrease in temperature with height in the troposphere is:
solution:
The troposphere is not heated from above by the Sun; it is heated from below, by longwave radiation given off by the Earth's surface.
Going up, air pressure and therefore density fall, so a given volume of air holds fewer molecules to absorb and retain that heat, and rising air expands and cools.
The Earth's distance from the Sun changes by a few kilometres out of 150 million, which cannot account for a fall of tens of degrees over 12 km.
Absorption of ultraviolet radiation warms the stratosphere, not the troposphere, and water vapour thins with height but is never absent.
The controlling factor is therefore the decrease in pressure with height.
Matches option A.
subject: Geography

stem: Which one of the following is the correct sequence of atmospheric layers from Earth’s surface upward?
solution:
Order the shells upward from the surface by the sign of the temperature gradient in each:
Troposphere, 0 to about 12 km, temperature falls.
Stratosphere, to about 50 km, temperature rises because ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation.
Mesosphere, to about 80 km, temperature falls again to the coldest point in the atmosphere.
Thermosphere, above 80 km, temperature rises steeply.
Sequence: Troposphere, Stratosphere, Mesosphere, Thermosphere.
Matches option A.
subject: Geography

stem:
Consider the following statements about Coriolis force:
It is zero at the Equator.
It increases from Equator towards the Poles.
It directly determines wind speed.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
solution:
The Coriolis force per unit mass is \(2\Omega v \sin\phi\), where \(\phi\) is the latitude.
Statement 1: at the Equator \(\phi = 0\), so \(\sin\phi = 0\) and the force is zero. Correct.
Statement 2: \(\sin\phi\) rises from 0 at the Equator to 1 at the Poles, so the force increases poleward. Correct.
Statement 3: the Coriolis force acts at right angles to the motion, so it does no work and cannot change the speed of the wind; it only deflects its direction. Wind speed is set by the pressure gradient. Incorrect.
Correct statements: 1 and 2 only.
Matches option A.
subject: Geography

stem: In which layer of the atmosphere do meteors generally burn up?
solution:
A meteor burns up where the air is still thin enough for it to have survived the layers above, yet dense enough for friction to heat it to incandescence.
That happens between about 80 km and 50 km above the surface, which is the mesosphere.
Above it the thermosphere is too rarefied to produce the friction; below it the stratosphere and troposphere are reached only by the largest bodies.
Matches option B.
subject: Geography

stem: Albedo refers to the:
optB: Reflection of solar radiation by Earth
solution:
Albedo is defined as the fraction of the incoming solar radiation that a surface throws back:
albedo = reflected radiation / incident radiation, usually quoted as a percentage.
Fresh snow returns most of what falls on it, so its albedo is high; the Earth as a whole has an albedo of about 30 per cent.
It is a measure of reflection, not of absorption, of emission, or of scattering within the air.
Matches option B.
subject: Geography

stem: Which of the following best explains why upper atmosphere is warmer during daytime?
solution:
The upper atmosphere, the thermosphere, cannot take its heat from the ground, which is far below and radiates in the longwave.
It is the first part of the atmosphere the solar beam meets, and there the scarce molecules absorb the high-energy ultraviolet and X-ray portion of that beam.
Each absorption puts a large amount of energy into very few particles, so the kinetic temperature rises steeply during daylight.
Conduction from below is negligible in so rarefied a gas, and water vapour never reaches that height.
Matches option B.
subject: Geography

stem: Which one of the following is NOT a greenhouse gas?
solution:
A greenhouse gas must absorb longwave (infrared) radiation, which requires a molecule whose vibration changes its dipole moment.
Methane, carbon dioxide and nitrous oxide all satisfy this and are listed greenhouse gases.
Nitrogen is a symmetrical diatomic molecule with no dipole moment, so it is transparent to infrared radiation and is not a greenhouse gas, despite forming 78 per cent of the air.
Matches option D.
subject: Geography

stem: Which one of the following contains the highest percentage of atmospheric mass?
solution:
Atmospheric pressure falls roughly exponentially with height, so most of the mass lies in the lowest shell.
The troposphere reaches only about 12 km yet contains about 75 to 80 per cent of the total mass of the atmosphere, along with almost all its water vapour and dust.
The stratosphere, mesosphere and thermosphere together hold the small remainder.
Matches option A.
subject: Geography

stem: Which one of the following correctly explains the absence of S-waves in the Earth’s outer core?
solution:
S-waves are transverse (shear) waves, and their speed is \(v_{s}=\sqrt{\mu/\rho}\), where \(\mu\) is the rigidity modulus of the medium.
A liquid cannot resist shear, so for a liquid \(\mu = 0\) and hence \(v_{s} = 0\): no S-wave can pass through it at all.
Seismographs record an S-wave shadow zone beyond about \(103^{\circ}\) of arc from the epicentre, and that absence is the classic proof that the outer core is molten.
High temperature and high pressure by themselves do not stop shear waves, since the inner core is both hotter and at greater pressure and does transmit them; magnetic properties have no bearing on elastic wave propagation.
Matches option C.
chapter: Earth's Structure, Landforms and Geological Time
subject: Geography

stem: Which one of the following gases is found in highest quantity in the exosphere?
solution:
In the exosphere the gas is so thin that molecules follow ballistic paths and the lightest escape most readily, so the composition is sorted by molecular mass.
Hydrogen, of relative molecular mass about 1, is the lightest and comes to dominate the outermost shell, with helium next.
Nitrogen and oxygen are far heavier and are left behind in the layers below.
Matches option A.
subject: Geography

stem: Which one of the following gases is placed second in respect of abundance in the Earth's atmosphere?
solution:
By volume, dry air is about 78.08 per cent nitrogen and about 20.95 per cent oxygen, with argon third at about 0.93 per cent and carbon dioxide far smaller.
Nitrogen is therefore first in abundance and oxygen second.
Hydrogen is present only in traces near the surface.
Matches option A.
subject: Geography

stem: Dinitrogen (\(\text{N}_2\)) and dioxygen (\(\text{O}_2\)) are the main constituents of air but they do not react with each other to form oxides of nitrogen because:
optA: The reaction requires initiation by a catalyst
optC: The reaction is endothermic and requires very high temperature
optD: The stoichiometry of \(\text{N}_2\) and \(\text{O}_2\) in air is not ideal for the reaction to take place
solution:
For \(\text{N}_2 + \text{O}_2 \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NO}\), \(\Delta H = +180\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\), so the reaction is strongly endothermic.
The nitrogen molecule is also held by a triple bond of about \(946\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\), one of the strongest known.
An endothermic reaction behind so high a barrier does not proceed at ordinary atmospheric temperatures; it needs the very high temperature of a lightning stroke or an internal-combustion engine, where nitric oxide does in fact form.
The oxides of nitrogen are not the obstacle, nor is the mixing ratio of the two gases, and air contains no catalyst that brings the reaction about.
Matches option C.
subject: Geography

stem: Which one of the following is the correct sequence of atmospheric layers as we move from the Earth's surface upwards?
solution:
Counting upward from the ground: Troposphere, then Stratosphere, then Mesosphere, then Thermosphere.
The ozone layer lies in the second of these, and the coldest point of the whole atmosphere, the mesopause, sits at the top of the third.
Sequence: Troposphere, Stratosphere, Mesosphere, Thermosphere.
Matches option B.
subject: Geography

stem: The normal lapse rate of temperature of Earth's atmosphere drops to \(0^\circ\text{C}\) at the:
solution:
The subject of the statement is the normal lapse rate, that is the rate at which temperature falls with height inside the troposphere, about \(6.5^{\circ}\text{C}\) per kilometre.
That fall does not continue indefinitely. At the top of the troposphere the temperature stops decreasing, so the rate itself falls to zero and the layer becomes isothermal; that isothermal cap is the tropopause.
Immediately above it, in the stratosphere, the gradient reverses and temperature begins to rise with height, so the normal lapse rate has already ended by then.
The lapse rate is therefore extinguished at the upper boundary of the tropopause.
Matches option B.
subject: Geography

stem: In which one of the following layers of the atmosphere do all weather phenomena occur?
solution:
Weather needs water vapour, dust nuclei and vertical mixing.
All three are confined to the lowest shell: the troposphere holds about 99 per cent of the atmosphere's water vapour and nearly all its dust, and, because temperature falls with height there, it is convectively unstable.
Clouds, rain, storms and fog therefore all form in the troposphere; the layers above it are dry and stable.
Matches option B.
subject: Geography

stem:
Consider the following statements with reference to the structure of the Earth's atmosphere:
Thickness of the troposphere is greatest at the equator.
The air temperature of the tropopause is highest above the poles.
The temperature in the troposphere decreases at the rate of \(1^\circ\text{F}\) for every 165 m of height.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution:
Statement 1: the troposphere is deepest over the equator, about 18 km, and shallowest over the poles, about 8 km, because strong equatorial heating drives convection higher. Correct.
Statement 2: the tropopause is coldest over the equator, about \(-80^{\circ}\text{C}\), and warmest over the poles, about \(-45^{\circ}\text{C}\), so its temperature is highest above the poles. Correct.
Statement 3: the figure normally quoted is a fall of \(1^{\circ}\text{C}\) for every 165 m, which works out at \(1000/165 \approx 6^{\circ}\text{C}\) per km, the normal lapse rate. As printed the statement gives \(1^{\circ}\text{F}\) for every 165 m, and \(1^{\circ}\text{F} = 0.56^{\circ}\text{C}\), so it claims only about \(3.4^{\circ}\text{C}\) per km, roughly half the true rate. Incorrect.
Correct statements: 1 and 2 only.
Matches option B.
subject: Geography

stem: Which one of the following statements about temperature is correct?
optA: Temperature decreases with height in the stratosphere
optB: Temperature is constant at different heights in the stratosphere
optC: Temperature increases with height in the troposphere at an average rate of \(6.5^\circ\text{C}\) per kilometre
optD: Temperature decreases with height in the troposphere at an average rate of \(6.4^\circ\text{C}\) per kilometre
solution:
[PRINTED DEFECT] No printed option is both correct in value and correct in direction. One option carries the standard lapse rate but states that temperature rises; another states the direction correctly with a non-standard value.

Test each statement against the known vertical temperature profile.
In the stratosphere temperature rises with height, from about \(-55^{\circ}\text{C}\) at the tropopause to near \(0^{\circ}\text{C}\) at the stratopause, because ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation there. So a claim that it decreases in the stratosphere is false, and a claim that it stays constant there is false as well.
In the troposphere temperature falls with height, so a claim that it increases in the troposphere is false whatever rate is attached to it: the direction is already wrong.
The one remaining statement has the direction right, a decrease with height in the troposphere, and gives \(6.4^{\circ}\text{C}\) per kilometre, which lies inside the range textbooks quote for the normal lapse rate (most commonly \(6.5^{\circ}\text{C}\) per km).
It is the only one of the four statements whose claim is true.
Matches option D.
reviewNote: Defective as printed: no option states the standard normal lapse rate correctly. The option carrying the standard value \(6.5^{\circ}\text{C}\) per km states the wrong DIRECTION (an increase with height in the troposphere), which makes its claim categorically false; the option keyed here has the direction right and gives \(6.4^{\circ}\text{C}\) per km, a value that differs from the usual 6.5 but lies within the range textbooks quote and does not make the statement false. Adjudicated to the only option whose claim is true as printed. A student who matched on the number 6.5 and ignored the direction has a reasonable grievance; the setter should correct the wording to 'decreases ... 6.5'.
subject: Geography

stem: When heat rays are reflected from the Earth, gases like carbon dioxide and nitrous oxide do not allow them to escape back into space, causing our planet to heat up. These gases are known as:
solution:
The gases named absorb the longwave heat radiation leaving the Earth and re-radiate part of it downward, so heat is trapped below and the surface warms.
That trapping is the greenhouse effect, and the gases responsible for it, mainly water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide and ozone, are called greenhouse gases.
The noble gases are chemically inert and infrared-transparent, and the other two names are not terms used in atmospheric science.
Matches option B.
subject: Geography

stem: Which one of the following is not a greenhouse gas?
solution:
Water vapour, methane and ozone all absorb infrared radiation and are counted among the greenhouse gases.
Carbon monoxide absorbs only very weakly in the infrared window and is not classed as a direct greenhouse gas; it is treated as an indirect one, because by consuming hydroxyl radicals it lengthens the atmospheric life of methane.
The gas that is not a greenhouse gas is therefore carbon monoxide.
Matches option D.
subject: Geography

stem: Which one of the following greenhouse gases is present in the largest concentration in the atmosphere?
subject: Geography

stem: The Earth's atmosphere is mainly heated by which one of the following?
solution:
Incoming solar radiation is shortwave, and the atmosphere is largely transparent to it, so most of it passes through and is absorbed at the ground.
The heated ground then emits longwave (infrared) terrestrial radiation, and water vapour and carbon dioxide absorb that strongly.
The atmosphere is therefore warmed from below, by longwave terrestrial radiation, and not directly by the solar beam that it mostly lets through.
Matches option C.
subject: Geography

stem: Which one of the following is not a main greenhouse gas?
solution:
Water vapour, carbon dioxide and methane are all infrared-active and are main greenhouse gases; water vapour is the largest single contributor.
Oxygen is a symmetrical diatomic molecule whose vibration produces no change of dipole moment, so it cannot absorb infrared radiation and is not a greenhouse gas.
Matches option B.
subject: Geography

stem: What happens when sunlight travels through the Earth's atmosphere?
optA: The blue colour is scattered more compared to the red colour
optB: The red colour is scattered more compared to the blue colour
optC: Both the blue and the red colours are scattered equally
optD: The blue colour is not scattered but the red colour is scattered the most
solution:
Rayleigh scattering by air molecules varies as \(1/\lambda^{4}\), so the shorter the wavelength the stronger the scattering.
Blue light has \(\lambda \approx 450\ \text{nm}\) and red \(\lambda \approx 700\ \text{nm}\), so the ratio of scattering is \((700/450)^{4} \approx 5.9\).
Blue is therefore scattered nearly six times as strongly as red, which is why the daytime sky is blue and the low Sun looks red.
Matches option A.
subject: Geography

stem:
One of the main causes of air pollution in cities is emissions from vehicles like cars and trucks. Cars emit various pollutants which are harmful to human health when inhaled, such as:
1. Nitrogen oxides (\(\text{NO}_x\))
2. Carbon monoxide (CO)
3. Carbon dioxide (\(\text{CO}_2\))
4. Benzene
Which of the above pollutants are not tolerated by human beings even at very low levels?
solution:
Judge each pollutant by whether it harms a human being at very low concentration.
Nitrogen oxides irritate and damage the lining of the lung at a fraction of a part per million.
Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin about 240 times more strongly than oxygen, so even a few hundred parts per million is dangerous.
Benzene is a proven carcinogen for which no threshold of safe exposure is recognised.
Carbon dioxide, by contrast, is a natural constituent of air that we breathe out continuously; it is harmful only at concentrations of several per cent, not at low levels.
Not tolerated even at very low levels: 1, 2 and 4.
Matches option D.
subject: Geography

stem: Which one of the following is a cause of acid rain?
solution:
Acid rain forms when an acidic oxide dissolves in atmospheric moisture.
Sulphur dioxide released by burning coal and oil dissolves and oxidises to sulphurous and then sulphuric acid, \(\text{SO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{SO}_3\), and this is the chief cause, with oxides of nitrogen second.
Ammonia is basic and neutralises acidity; carbon monoxide is a neutral oxide that forms no acid with water; ozone is an oxidant but is not itself an acid-former.
Matches option C.
subject: Geography

stem: The poisonous nature of carbon monoxide (CO) is due to its:
optB: Ability to form a complex with haemoglobin
optC: Ability to reduce some metal oxides
optD: Property of having one sigma bond
solution:
Carbon monoxide binds to the iron of haemoglobin to form carboxyhaemoglobin, and its affinity for that site is about 240 times that of oxygen.
The occupied sites can no longer carry oxygen, and the complex is stable enough that the blood does not release it readily, so the tissues are starved of oxygen.
Its insolubility in water, its use as a reducing agent for metal oxides, and the bonding within the molecule have nothing to do with its toxicity.
Matches option B.
subject: Geography

stem: Which one of the following is the usual unit of measurement for air pressure used in India?
solution:
Air pressure is a force per unit area, so its unit must carry those dimensions.
Indian meteorological practice states surface pressure in millibars, where \(1\ \text{millibar} = 100\ \text{pascal}\) and standard sea-level pressure is 1013.25 millibar.
A centimetre measures length, a milligram mass and a millilitre volume, so none of them can measure pressure.
Matches option B.
subject: Geography

stem:
With reference to the 'Coriolis force', which statements are correct?
1. It increases with increase in wind velocity.
2. It is maximum at the poles and is absent at the equator.
solution:
The Coriolis force per unit mass is \(2\Omega v \sin\phi\).
Statement 1: the expression is directly proportional to \(v\), so the force increases as the wind velocity increases. Correct.
Statement 2: \(\sin\phi = 0\) at the equator and \(\sin\phi = 1\) at the poles, so the force is absent at the equator and maximum at the poles. Correct.
Both statements are correct.
Matches option C.
subject: Geography

stem:
Consider the following statements:
S1: Incoming solar radiation is mostly visible and shortwave radiation.
S2: Terrestrial radiation emitted by Earth is mostly longwave infrared radiation.
S3: The atmosphere is more transparent to terrestrial radiation than incoming solar radiation.
solution:
S1: the Sun radiates at about 6000 K, so its output peaks in the visible and is shortwave. Correct.
S2: the Earth radiates at about 288 K, so its output peaks near 10 micrometres and is longwave infrared. Correct.
S3: the atmosphere lets most of the shortwave solar beam through, while its water vapour and carbon dioxide absorb the outgoing longwave strongly; it is therefore more transparent to solar radiation than to terrestrial radiation, the reverse of what is stated. Incorrect.
Correct statements: 1 and 2 only.
Matches option A.
subject: Geography

stem:
S1: Atmosphere is heated more by incoming solar radiation than terrestrial radiation.
S2: Carbon dioxide and greenhouse gases are good absorbers of longwave radiation.
optA: Both correct and S2 explains S1
optB: Both correct but S2 doesn't explain S1
solution:
S1: the atmosphere is largely transparent to incoming shortwave solar radiation, which passes through to be absorbed at the ground, and it is then heated from below by the longwave terrestrial radiation the ground emits. It is heated more by terrestrial radiation, so S1 is incorrect.
S2: carbon dioxide, water vapour and the other greenhouse gases absorb strongly in the infrared, so they are good absorbers of longwave radiation. S2 is correct.
Verdict: S1 incorrect, S2 correct. S2 is in fact the reason S1 is false.
Matches option D.
subject: Geography

stem:
Which statements regarding insolation are correct?
S1: Insolation is predominantly short-wave radiation.
S2: Insolation is evenly distributed across Earth.
solution:
S1: insolation is the incoming solar radiation received at the Earth, and the Sun's surface is at about 6000 K, so it is predominantly shortwave. Correct.
S2: the amount received falls from the equator to the poles, because at high latitudes the beam strikes obliquely and travels a longer path through the atmosphere, so its distribution is markedly uneven. Incorrect.
Only S1 is correct.
Matches option A.
subject: Geography

stem: Which surface has the highest albedo?
subject: Geography

stem:
Which statements concerning Earth's atmosphere are correct?
S1: In stratosphere, temperature increases with altitude.
S2: In mesosphere, temperature decreases with altitude.
S3: Lowest atmospheric temperature recorded in upper mesosphere.
S4: Tropopause is an isothermal zone.
solution:
S1: in the stratosphere ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation, so temperature rises with altitude, from about \(-55^{\circ}\text{C}\) to near \(0^{\circ}\text{C}\). Correct.
S2: above the stratopause there is no ozone heating, so in the mesosphere temperature falls with altitude. Correct.
S3: that fall continues to the mesopause at about 80 km, where about \(-90^{\circ}\text{C}\) is reached, the lowest temperature anywhere in the atmosphere. Correct.
S4: at the tropopause the temperature ceases to fall and stays nearly steady with height, so it is an isothermal zone. Correct.
All four statements are correct.
Matches option D.
subject: Geography

stem: Isotherms are lines connecting points having same:
solution:
An isopleth joins places having an equal value of some element, and the prefix names the element.
Iso- with -therm (Greek therme, heat) gives lines of equal temperature.
Lines of equal pressure are isobars, of equal humidity isohumes, of equal wind speed isotachs, so none of those belongs to isotherms.
Matches option C.
subject: Geography

stem:
Consider the following statements:
1. Half the water vapour in atmosphere lies below 1000 m.
2. Amount of precipitable water increases from equator to pole.
solution:
Statement 1: water vapour is supplied by the surface and removed by condensation, so its density decays rapidly with height, and roughly half of the total column moisture lies within about the first kilometre of the ground. Taken as correct.
Statement 2: precipitable water depends on temperature through the saturation vapour pressure, which falls steeply as air gets colder. It is therefore greatest over the warm equator, about 40 to 50 mm, and least over the cold poles, a few millimetres, so it decreases from equator to pole rather than increasing. Incorrect.
Only statement 1 is correct.
Matches option A.
reviewNote: Statement 1's figure is approximate and is worth checking with the setter. Standard moisture profiles put the half-column level of atmospheric water vapour nearer 1.4 to 1.6 km than 1000 m, and several textbooks give the figure as 'below 2000 m'. The letter does not turn on it here, because statement 2 is unambiguously false (precipitable water DECREASES from equator to pole), so the only live options are 'Only 1' and 'Neither 1 nor 2'. Keyed on the reading that statement 1 is the intended textbook approximation; an existing bank row carrying the identical question is keyed the same way.
subject: Geography

stem: UV rays are mostly prevented from reaching land surface as they are absorbed mostly by:
solution:
Ultraviolet radiation is absorbed by ozone, and the ozone layer lies between about 15 km and 35 km, inside the stratosphere.
There ozone is continually split and reformed, \(\text{O}_3 + \text{UV} \rightarrow \text{O}_2 + \text{O}\), and the energy taken up both screens the surface and warms that layer.
The troposphere below, and the mesosphere and thermosphere above, carry no such concentration of ozone.
Matches option D.
subject: Geography

stem: Jet streams are usually found in:
solution:
Jet streams are narrow ribbons of very fast westerly wind, driven by the steep temperature gradient between neighbouring air masses.
They form where that gradient is sharpest and friction is least, in the upper troposphere at about 9 km to 12 km, which is the level of the tropopause.
The ozonosphere lies far above them, and the mesosphere and ionosphere higher still.
Matches option C.
subject: Geography

stem: Which one of the following statements regarding the Stratosphere layer of the atmosphere is not correct?
optA: Temperature increases with an increase in altitude within this layer.
optB: It is almost completely free from clouds and associated weather phenomena.
optC: It extends upwards to a height of about 50 km from the Earth's surface.
optD: The highest concentration of water vapour in the atmosphere is found in this layer.
solution:
The question asks which statement is not correct, so test each in turn.
Temperature does increase with altitude in the stratosphere, because ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation there. True as stated.
The stratosphere is dry and stable, so it is almost free of clouds and weather. True as stated.
It extends from the tropopause up to the stratopause at about 50 km. True as stated.
Water vapour, however, is concentrated near its source at the ground: about 99 per cent of it lies in the troposphere, and the stratosphere is one of the driest parts of the atmosphere. That statement is false.
Matches option D.
subject: Geography

stem:
Consider the following statements regarding Insolation and Terrestrial Radiation:
1. The Earth's atmosphere is heated more by incoming shortwave solar radiation than by longwave terrestrial radiation.
2. Carbon dioxide (\(\text{CO}_2\)) and water vapour are transparent to incoming solar radiation but absorb outgoing terrestrial radiation.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution:
Statement 1: the atmosphere is largely transparent to the shortwave solar beam, which passes through to heat the ground, and is then warmed from below by longwave terrestrial radiation. It is heated more by terrestrial radiation, so the statement reverses the truth. Incorrect.
Statement 2: carbon dioxide and water vapour transmit shortwave solar radiation but absorb strongly in the infrared, so they trap the outgoing terrestrial radiation. This selective behaviour is the greenhouse effect. Correct.
Only statement 2 is correct.
Matches option B.
subject: Geography

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. The \(\underline{\text{brave}}\) soldier fought valiantly.
solution:
The underlined word stands before the noun 'soldier' and tells what kind of soldier he is.
A word that qualifies a noun is an adjective.
Matches option B.
subject: English

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. She \(\underline{\text{runs}}\) faster than anyone else.
solution:
The underlined word states the action performed by the subject 'She' and carries the tense and the third-person -s ending.
A word that asserts an action about a subject is a verb.
Matches option B.
subject: English

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. \(\underline{\text{Wow}}\), what a beautiful sunset!
solution:
The underlined word stands outside the grammar of the sentence, takes no subject and links to nothing; it simply blurts out sudden feeling, here delight.
Such an exclamatory word is an interjection.
Matches option A.
subject: English

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. The book \(\underline{\text{on}}\) the table is mine.
solution:
The underlined word stands before the noun phrase 'the table' and shows the position of the book in relation to it.
A word that governs a noun and shows its relation to another word is a preposition.
Matches option B.
subject: English

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. \(\underline{\text{They}}\) are my best friends.
solution:
The underlined word is the subject of 'are' and stands in place of the names of the people concerned.
A word used instead of a noun is a pronoun.
Matches option A.
subject: English

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. He speaks \(\underline{\text{confidently}}\) in public.
solution:
The underlined word tells how he speaks, so it modifies the verb 'speaks'.
A word that modifies a verb is an adverb; the -ly ending on the adjective 'confident' is the regular mark of one.
Matches option C.
subject: English

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. This is the \(\underline{\text{largest}}\) diamond in Asia.
solution:
The underlined word stands between 'the' and the noun 'diamond' and tells which diamond is meant.
It is the superlative degree of 'large', and a word that qualifies a noun is an adjective.
Matches option B.
subject: English

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. \(\underline{\text{And}}\) then the story ended happily.
solution:
The underlined word opens the sentence but joins its statement to what has gone before; it names nothing and modifies nothing.
A joining word of this kind is a conjunction.
Matches option A.
subject: English

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. The \(\underline{\text{cat}}\) jumped over the wall.
solution:
The underlined word names an animal and is the subject of the verb 'jumped'.
A naming word is a noun.
Matches option C.
subject: English

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. She arrived \(\underline{\text{early}}\) for the exam.
solution:
The underlined word tells when she arrived, so it modifies the verb 'arrived'.
A word that modifies a verb is an adverb. The same word is an adjective in 'an early train', where it would qualify a noun, but here it does not.
Matches option C.
subject: English

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. \(\underline{\text{Our}}\) house is near the school.
solution:
The underlined word stands before the noun 'house' and tells whose house it is, so it is qualifying that noun rather than replacing it.
Words of this kind (my, our, your, his, her, its, their) are possessive adjectives.
Matches option B.
subject: English

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. He \(\underline{\text{writes}}\) neatly and clearly.
solution:
The underlined word states the action performed by the subject 'He' and carries the tense.
A word that asserts an action about a subject is a verb; the two -ly words that follow modify it.
Matches option B.
subject: English

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. The \(\underline{\text{old}}\) man walked slowly.
solution:
The underlined word stands between 'The' and the noun 'man' and tells what kind of man he is.
A word that qualifies a noun is an adjective.
Matches option C.
subject: English

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. \(\underline{\text{Alas}}\), we lost the match!
solution:
[PRINTED DEFECT] The printed option LABELS are defective: the second and third options are both lettered B, and there is no C. A student who intends the third option shades B and is credited for the second. The OMR must accept both B-lettered slots, or the question must be dropped.

The underlined word stands outside the grammar of the sentence, takes no subject and joins nothing; it merely voices sudden sorrow at the loss.
Such an exclamatory word is an interjection.
Matches option B.
subject: English
reviewNote: Printed defect in the OPTION LABELS, not in the answer. The page prints the four labels as A) B) B) D) - there is no C) and the letter B) appears twice. The correct option text, 'Interjection', is the SECOND of the four printed left to right, and that slot carries the printed label B), so 'B' is the letter to key. The risk on the OMR is that the THIRD slot ('Pronoun', wrong) is also printed B), so a student who chose Pronoun would bubble B as well and would be credited by accident. The setter must re-letter the options before this paper is reused.

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. Put the keys \(\underline{\text{in}}\) the drawer.
solution:
The underlined word stands before the noun phrase 'the drawer' and shows where the keys are to go in relation to it.
A word that governs a noun and shows its relation to another word is a preposition.
Matches option C.
subject: English

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. \(\underline{\text{Quickly}}\), finish your homework.
solution:
The underlined word tells how the homework is to be finished, so it modifies the imperative verb 'finish'.
A word that modifies a verb is an adverb; its position at the head of the sentence does not change its class.
Matches option C.
subject: English

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. Mumbai is the \(\underline{\text{busiest}}\) city in India.
solution:
The underlined word stands between 'the' and the noun 'city' and tells which city is meant.
It is the superlative degree of 'busy', and a word that qualifies a noun is an adjective.
Matches option C.
subject: English

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. \(\underline{\text{Either}}\) tea or coffee is fine.
solution:
The underlined word is the first half of the pair 'either ... or', which joins the two alternatives 'tea' and 'coffee'.
A word that joins words or clauses is a conjunction; 'either ... or' is a correlative conjunction.
Matches option A.
subject: English

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. The \(\underline{\text{dog}}\) barked loudly at night.
solution:
The underlined word names an animal and is the subject of the verb 'barked'.
A naming word is a noun.
Matches option B.
subject: English

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. She sings \(\underline{\text{beautifully}}\) on stage.
solution:
The underlined word tells how she sings, so it modifies the verb 'sings'.
A word that modifies a verb is an adverb.
Matches option C.
subject: English

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. \(\underline{\text{This}}\) book is more useful than that one.
solution:
The underlined word stands immediately before the noun 'book' and points out which book is meant, so it is introducing the noun, not standing in place of it.
A demonstrative used before a noun is a determiner; it would be a demonstrative pronoun only if it stood alone, as 'that one' does later in the same sentence.
Matches option B.
subject: English

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. She is \(\underline{\text{very}}\) intelligent for her age.
solution:
The underlined word modifies the adjective 'intelligent' and does nothing but raise its degree.
A degree word used to strengthen an adjective in this way is an intensifier; it says nothing about time.
Matches option A.
subject: English

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. He worked hard \(\underline{\text{because}}\) he wanted to succeed.
solution:
The underlined word joins the main clause 'He worked hard' to the clause 'he wanted to succeed' and makes the second one subordinate, giving the reason.
A word that joins clauses in this way is a conjunction.
Matches option B.
subject: English

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. The man \(\underline{\text{who}}\) lives next door is a pilot.
solution:
The underlined word introduces the clause 'lives next door', which describes the noun 'man', and at the same time acts as the subject of 'lives'.
A pronoun that both refers back to a noun and introduces a clause describing it is a relative pronoun; its antecedent is 'man'.
Matches option B.
subject: English

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. \(\underline{\text{Swimming}}\) is a good exercise for all ages.
solution:
The underlined word is an -ing form standing as the subject of the verb 'is', the position a noun would occupy ('Exercise is good').
An -ing form doing the work of a noun is a gerund; it is not a present participle, because it qualifies no noun and forms no continuous tense.
Matches option B.
subject: English

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. The \(\underline{\text{broken}}\) window was repaired yesterday.
solution:
The underlined word is the third form of the verb 'break' and stands before the noun 'window', telling what kind of window it was; the window received the action rather than performed it.
A verb form in -en or -ed used in this passive, adjectival way is a past participle.
Matches option C.
subject: English

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. He kept \(\underline{\text{talking}}\) despite repeated warnings.
solution:
The underlined word is an -ing form following the finite verb 'kept'; it qualifies no noun and forms no continuous tense, so it is not doing a participle's work.
It completes 'kept' in the position an object noun would fill, and 'keep' belongs to the set of verbs (keep, enjoy, avoid, finish, mind, stop) that are followed by the -ing noun-form of the verb.
An -ing form doing the work of a noun is a gerund.
Matches option A.
subject: English
reviewNote: Analytically contested, though the answer is the one an Indian syllabus expects. 'keep' is on the standard list of verbs followed by the -ing noun-form (keep, enjoy, avoid, finish, mind, stop), and by the school test the word is neither qualifying a noun nor forming a continuous tense, which leaves gerund. A descriptive-grammar analysis would object that 'keep' also takes a plain adjective ('He kept quiet'), which suggests the -ing form here is a predicative complement, i.e. a present participle. Keyed 'Gerund' on the syllabus convention; flag it if the setter wants the participle reading.

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. There isn’t \(\underline{\text{any}}\) sugar left in the jar.
solution:
The underlined word stands before the noun 'sugar' and limits its quantity without describing it.
A word used before a noun to introduce and limit it in this way is a determiner; here it is the quantifier used with a negative verb.
Matches option B.
subject: English

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. They were \(\underline{\text{too}}\) tired to continue the march.
solution:
The underlined word modifies the adjective 'tired' and does nothing but raise its degree, to the point where continuing becomes impossible.
A degree word used to strengthen an adjective in this way is an intensifier.
Matches option A.
subject: English

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. You must choose \(\underline{\text{either}}\) this road or that one.
solution:
The underlined word is the first half of the pair 'either ... or', which joins the two alternatives 'this road' and 'that one'.
It is not determining the noun 'road', because 'this' already does that; it is joining the alternatives.
A word that joins words or clauses is a conjunction, and 'either ... or' is a correlative conjunction.
Matches option A.
subject: English

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. I stayed at home \(\underline{\text{although}}\) it was a holiday.
solution:
The underlined word joins the clause 'it was a holiday' to the main clause 'I stayed at home' and makes it subordinate, expressing concession.
A word that joins clauses in this way is a conjunction; a preposition would be followed by a noun, not by a clause with its own subject and verb.
Matches option B.
subject: English

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. The girl \(\underline{\text{whose}}\) phone was stolen reported it to the police.
solution:
The underlined word introduces the clause 'phone was stolen', which describes the noun 'girl', and at the same time shows that the phone belongs to her.
A pronoun that refers back to a noun, introduces a clause describing it, and stands in the possessive case is a relative pronoun.
Matches option B.
subject: English

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. \(\underline{\text{Reading}}\) novels improves your imagination.
solution:
The underlined word is an -ing form heading 'Reading novels', which is the subject of the verb 'improves' and occupies the position a noun would take.
An -ing form doing the work of a noun is a gerund; note that it keeps its verbal power and takes the object 'novels'.
Matches option A.
subject: English

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. The \(\underline{\text{fallen}}\) leaves covered the entire ground.
solution:
The underlined word is the third form of the verb 'fall' and stands before the noun 'leaves', telling which leaves are meant.
A verb form in -en or -ed used in this adjectival way is a past participle.
Matches option C.
subject: English

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. The children, \(\underline{\text{playing}}\) in the garden, did not hear the bell.
solution:
The underlined word heads the phrase 'playing in the garden', set off by commas, which describes the noun 'children'.
An -ing form that qualifies a noun instead of naming an action is a present participle; a gerund would occupy a noun's place in the sentence, and this phrase does not.
Matches option B.
subject: English

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. \(\underline{\text{Several}}\) students failed to submit the assignment.
solution:
The underlined word stands before the noun 'students' and states how many without describing what kind they are.
A word used before a noun to introduce and quantify it is a determiner; an adjective of quality would answer 'what kind', which this does not.
Matches option A.
subject: English

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. She is \(\underline{\text{so}}\) tired that she cannot walk.
solution:
The underlined word modifies the adjective 'tired' and raises its degree, the result of that degree being given by the clause that follows.
A degree word used to strengthen an adjective in this way is an intensifier; the joining work in the sentence is done by 'that', not by the underlined word.
Matches option A.
subject: English

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. He was late, \(\underline{\text{so}}\) he missed the beginning of the lecture.
solution:
The underlined word stands between two complete statements, 'He was late' and 'he missed the beginning of the lecture', and joins them, showing the second as the consequence of the first.
It modifies no adjective or adverb, so it is not a degree word; a word that joins two clauses of equal rank is a conjunction.
Matches option B.
subject: English

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. The car \(\underline{\text{that}}\) he bought is very expensive.
solution:
The underlined word introduces the clause 'he bought', which describes the noun 'car', and acts as the object of 'bought' inside that clause.
A word that refers back to a noun and introduces a clause describing it is a relative pronoun; it is not pointing anything out, as a demonstrative would.
Matches option B.
subject: English

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. We saw a \(\underline{\text{burning}}\) house on the hill.
solution:
The underlined word is an -ing form standing before the noun 'house' and telling what kind of house was seen; the house is performing the action of burning.
An -ing form that qualifies a noun in this active way is a present participle.
Matches option C.
subject: English

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. \(\underline{\text{Whichever}}\) option you choose will affect the entire team.
solution:
The underlined word stands immediately before the noun 'option' and selects which option is meant.
A relative pronoun stands in place of a noun and cannot be followed by its own noun, so the word here is functioning as a determiner (a relative determiner) over 'option'.
Matches option B.
subject: English
reviewNote: Judgement call worth a second eye. Many Indian grammar books (Wren and Martin among them) list 'whoever / whatever / whichever' under COMPOUND RELATIVE PRONOUNS, so a teacher could reasonably key the relative-pronoun option. Keyed 'Determiner' because in this sentence the word is followed immediately by its own noun, 'option', and a pronoun by definition stands in place of a noun rather than accompanying one; the same books treat this adjectival use as a relative ADJECTIVE. The paper is also internally consistent with that reading - Q61 ('This book'), Q68 ('any sugar') and Q76 ('Several students') are all keyed Determiner on exactly this test, and the Q61 reading is confirmed by an existing bank row. If the setter intends the pronoun reading, the sentence should drop the noun: 'Whichever you choose will affect the entire team.'

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. \(\underline{\text{Having finished}}\) the report, she submitted it to the commander.
solution:
The underlined words head the phrase 'Having finished the report', which has no finite verb and no subject of its own, and which tells when and why she acted, attaching to the subject 'she'.
The phrase is headed by 'having', the -ing form of 'have'; the construction is the perfect participle, an active form built on the present participle, so of the classes offered it belongs with the present participle phrase.
A past participle phrase would begin with the third form alone, as in 'Exhausted after the drill', and a gerund phrase would occupy a noun's place in the sentence, which this does not.
Matches option B.
subject: English
reviewNote: Strictly this is a PERFECT participle phrase, and no option names that class. It is keyed to the present participle phrase because the phrase is headed by 'Having', the -ing form of 'have', and because the perfect participle is an ACTIVE form, unlike the past participle phrase, which in this paper is illustrated separately by Q84 ('exhausted after the drill'). If the setter intends a three-way participle classification, the option list should be extended to name the perfect participle.

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. The officer was \(\underline{\text{so}}\) impressed by his conduct that he recommended him for promotion.
solution:
The underlined word modifies 'impressed' and does nothing but raise its degree; the clause that follows states the result of that degree.
A degree word used to strengthen in this way is an intensifier. The joining in the sentence is done by 'that', so the underlined word is not itself a conjunction of either kind.
Matches option A.
subject: English
reviewNote: Options (a) 'Intensifier' and (d) 'Degree adverb (not intensifier)' name overlapping categories, so the item is defective as printed. Keyed to 'Intensifier' for two reasons. First, internal consistency: Q77 puts the IDENTICAL 'so ... that' construction in front of the student with 'Intensifier' as the only tenable option, so the paper itself already treats 'so' before an adjective as an intensifier; and Q62 keys 'very' the same way. Second, 'so' before an adjective is a textbook intensifier, so the parenthetical denial in (d) is the part that is wrong. The setter should drop one of the two options.

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. The cadets, \(\underline{\text{exhausted}}\) after the drill, still completed the written test.
solution:
The underlined word is the third form of the verb 'exhaust' and heads a phrase set off by commas that describes the noun 'cadets'; the cadets received the action rather than performed it.
It cannot be the finite verb of the sentence, because 'completed' already is, and the sentence would fall apart without it.
A third form used in this adjectival way is a past participle used as an adjective.
Matches option B.
subject: English

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. \(\underline{\text{Whom}}\) you choose as your partner will determine your score in the exercise.
solution:
The whole group 'Whom you choose as your partner' is the subject of 'will determine', so the underlined word is not asking a question; it introduces that clause and at the same time serves as the object of 'choose' inside it.
A word that introduces a clause and functions as a pronoun within it is a relative pronoun; it is not demonstrative, since it points nothing out, and not reflexive, since it turns the action back on no one.
Matches option B.
subject: English
reviewNote: The sentence is non-standard as printed. 'Whom you choose as your partner' is a fused (nominal) relative clause serving as the subject of 'will determine', and standard usage heads such a clause with 'Whoever/Whomever', not 'Whom'; a bare 'Whom' normally needs an antecedent ('the cadet whom you choose'). No option describes a free relative, so it is keyed to the relative-pronoun option, which is the only one that gets both facts right - the word introduces a clause and functions as the object of 'choose' within it. The interrogative option is excluded by its own word 'only', and nothing here is demonstrative or reflexive. Recommend the setter change 'Whom' to 'Whomever' or supply an antecedent.

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. \(\underline{\text{That}}\) many cadets failed the test surprised the instructors.
optB: Subordinating conjunction introducing a noun clause
solution:
The underlined word introduces the group 'many cadets failed the test', which is a complete statement acting as the subject of 'surprised'.
It stands in place of nothing and has no antecedent, so it is not a pronoun, and it qualifies no noun, so it is not a determiner; its whole work is to turn a statement into a noun clause.
A word that does that is a subordinating conjunction.
Matches option B.
subject: English

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. \(\underline{\text{Few}}\) of the instructions were actually followed during the drill.
solution:
The underlined word is followed by 'of the instructions', not by a noun of its own, and it is the head of the subject of 'were followed'.
A quantifier standing on its own in a noun's place like this is working as a pronoun; it would be a determiner or adjective only if it stood directly before a noun, as in 'Few instructions were followed'.
Matches option B.
subject: English

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. \(\underline{\text{Walking}}\) rapidly in full gear improved their stamina.
solution:
The underlined word heads the group 'Walking rapidly in full gear', which is the subject of the verb 'improved' and occupies the position a noun would take.
An -ing form doing the work of a noun is a gerund; it qualifies no noun here, and it is not a finite verb, since 'improved' already is.
Matches option A.
subject: English

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. This is the cadet \(\underline{\text{whose}}\) performance the board praised in its report.
solution:
The underlined word introduces the clause 'performance the board praised', which describes the noun 'cadet', and at the same time shows that the performance belongs to the cadet.
A word that refers back to a noun, introduces a clause describing it, and stands in the possessive case is a relative pronoun showing possession; calling it merely a possessive determiner would miss the clause it introduces.
Matches option B.
subject: English

stem: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word. He spoke \(\underline{\text{too}}\) quickly for the back rows to understand him clearly.
solution:
The underlined word modifies the adverb 'quickly' and raises its degree, to the point where understanding became impossible.
A degree word used to strengthen in this way is an intensifier; it joins no clauses and qualifies no noun.
Matches option A.
subject: English
